title: Why Do We Sleep?
paragraphs: Given that we devote roughly a third of our lives to sleep, it is remarkable how long its purpose remained a puzzle. Today, sleep scientists and public health bodies broadly agree that adults require seven to nine hours a night, while children and adolescents, whose brains are still maturing, need substantially more.

Sleep is far from a uniform state of rest. Over the course of a night, the brain cycles through distinct stages in periods of approximately ninety minutes: light sleep gives way to deep, slow-wave sleep, which is in turn followed by REM sleep, characterised by rapid eye movements and most strongly associated with vivid dreaming.

Each stage appears to make its own contribution. Slow-wave sleep is linked to physical restoration and to memory consolidation, the process by which fragile new memories are stabilised and integrated with existing knowledge. Experiments in animals have further revealed that the brain flushes out metabolic waste far more efficiently during sleep, suggesting a protective role whose implications for human brain health are still being explored.

While an occasional sleepless night carries little lasting risk, persistent sleep deprivation takes a measurable toll. Concentration, memory and decision-making deteriorate, emotional regulation weakens, and chronic short sleep is associated with an elevated risk of a range of health conditions. Sleep, in short, is not idle time but an active process on which much of our daily functioning depends.
